svg.text: When it lets go, does it come back?

Every one of these cars gets pushed past the tire's fitted limit by the disturbance, and they all get pushed past it about equally often. What separates them is what happens next — and these are two real laps.
61% front
reached 13.4 deg of slip — and got round
13.4 deg
COMPLETED THE LAP
The nose gives up first. The car runs wide, and running
wide scrubs speed, which is what saves it.
47% front
reached 12.0 deg of slip — and did not
12.0 deg
off the road
LEFT THE ROAD
The tail gives up first. The car rotates, and rotating
points the tires further from where they need to be.
past the tire's fitted limit (>12 deg of slip)
Laps that left the fitted region
and how many ended off the road, of 120 laps
47% front
54% front
61% front
65% front
left the fit, recovered
left the fit, crashed
Same exposure. Opposite outcome.
The 61% car left the limit MORE often than
the 47% car — 18 laps against 16 — and
crashed once against thirteen.
So the fast car is not fragile because it runs closer to the edge. Both cars go over the edge about as often. It is fragile because going over is a one-way trip.
That is Season 2's understeer mechanism showing up as a robustness property rather than a lap-time one. A car that loses the front pushes wide and slows itself down; a car that loses
the rear rotates, and rotating puts the tires further from where they need to be, which rotates it more. One is a negative feedback loop and the other is a positive one.

[MEASURED] Episode 10's policy, DEPLOYED, nothing retrained - 120 rollouts per design, both disturbances - [ASSUMED] steering noise sigma 0.15, grip +/-20% per lap - left panel: two real laps, seed 2 of each

Both left-panel laps are simulation output, not drawings — same corner, same driver, same disturbance settings, different car. Amber marks the stretch where the tire was outside the region our data covers.
